title: HelmEdge - MoE routing & rope scaling deep dive
summary: Technical deep dive covering MoE routing cost tradeoffs, rope (RoPE) scaling effects across Llama/Mistral/Qwen, KV cache and batching strategies, quantization profiles, and deployment considerations for VPC/on-prem. SE committed to run targeted benchmarks with and without route caching and to share a perf spreadsheet and recommended config snippets for HelmEdge's 4k token mid-latency product use case.
topics: MoE routing overhead and expert dispatch
RoPE scaling between model families (Llama vs Mistral vs Qwen)
KV cache semantics and cold-start effects
VPC / on-prem networking and HBM constraints
action_items: Diego: Run 1hr MoE routing vs no-routing microbench on 8xA100 with HelmEdge sample workload, include top-k gating overhead numbers - due 2025-04-14
Sasha: Share Redwood MoE best-practices doc and sample config (route-cache, expert-replica hints) - due 2025-04-10
Priya: Export RoPE-scaling plots comparing Llama-2-13B, Mistral-7B-Instruct, and Qwen-7B at seq-lens 512/2048/4096 - due 2025-04-16
Markus: Provide example inference payloads and p99 latency SLOs, plus current infra topology (NIC/HBM sizes) - due 2025-04-09
next_steps: Schedule on-prem trial with Redwood Private week of 2025-04-21
Redwood to share perf spreadsheet + deck links (sent via email)
Customer to confirm internal security review owners for SOC2+KMS discussion
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-07
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~1h15m
Attendees: Sasha Park (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood Research), Anika Bose (CTO, HelmEdge), Markus Lind (ML Infra), Ruth Chen (Director AI)

[00:00:00] Sasha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to make this a hands-on convo, Diego and Priya from infra/research are here, we'll go deep on MoE routing costs and rope scaling. Anika, you mentioned prep materials — did you get a chance to share the sample payloads?

[00:00:35] Anika: Yeah sent a small bucket of things to Markus but i'll upload one more later, sorry for the delay, hectic week. Our main ask is low-mid latency chat at 2k - 4k tokens, and we're curious how MoE and different families behave cost-wise.

[00:01:20] Diego: Cool, this is exactly the kind of thing we like to benchmark. Quick agenda: routing overhead for MoE, dispatch & expert placement, RoPE scaling effects across Llama/Mistral/Qwen, kv-cache/batching impacts, then deployment constraints for your on-prem racks / VPC. Sound good?

[00:01:48] Markus: Yes, and we really need concrete numbers — not just asymptotics — because our billing model ties to GPU-minutes.

[00:02:15] Priya: One thing up front: MoE routing introduces two classes of overhead: the gating computation (small MLP to select experts) and the scatter/gather dispatch to experts which can be memory and kernel-bound. For large batch sizes those amortize, but for low-latency single-user flows they can dominate.

[00:02:55] Ruth: Can you explain the gating more — is it per-token? per-sequence?

[00:03:10] Priya: Good Q. Most modern MoE implementations do token-level gating, so every new token triggers a small routing MLP. There are tricks — route caching for repeated prefixes is one — but token-level gives highest model capacity. Note, route-cache is heuristics: for dialogue with lots of changes it helps less.

[00:03:45] Anika: Our workload is chatty but often repeats system prompts and initial context, so route-cache might help. But Markus is also worried about GPU memory fragmentation when we do expert replicas.

[00:04:14] Diego: On fragmentation — expert replica placement matters. If you replicate experts across devices to reduce cross-device shuffles, you pay in HBM; if you centralize, you pay in PCIe/NIC traffic. For your racks (you mentioned 8xA100 with 40GB HBM), we recommended a hybrid: replicate hottest experts and route others across via NCCL.

[00:04:48] Markus: That's the core trade and we need to see p99 latency differences. Have you measured routing overhead percentage specifically?

[00:05:05] Priya: In our internal benchmarks we saw gating + dispatch add between 8% and 40% latency overhead depending on sequence length and batch size. For single-token low-batch cases, it was closer to 25-40%. With batching and route-cache it fell to single digits. YMMV by model family.

[00:05:40] Sasha: Let's talk about model family differences — Llama, Mistral, Qwen — RoPE handling and parameterization matter a lot. Priya, can you summarize?

[00:05:55] Priya: Sure. Llama-style models use rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) with sin/cos application; their numerical stability under longer seq lengths depends on the original RoPE base and whether it's been scaled. Mistral tends to use smaller base frequencies and benefits from sequence length-aware scaling patches — but the point is rope scaling interacts with kv-cache memory sizes and attention kernel selection. Qwen has some implementation differences in the rotary math and can show different degradation curves at 4k+.

[00:06:35] Markus: In practice, for 4k tokens we'd expect x2 memory on kv-cache vs 2k, correct? So HBM is going to be tight.

[00:06:50] Diego: Roughly yes. Each key/value is proportional to seq_len * hidden_size * 2 (k + v) * sizeof(dtype). With quantization that changes slightly (e.g., 8-bit stored but cache may be stored in FP16 for speed). For Llama-2-13B at seq=4k, on 40GB HBM you'll start trimming batch size or moving to NVLink across devices.

[00:07:22] Anika: We push batched multi-user traffic though, so batching helps amortize MoE cost — our p95 is more important than single-user p99. How does that change guidance?

[00:07:38] Priya: If you can batch 8-16 requests with similar seq lengths, MoE gating cost is amortized and expert dispatch becomes more efficient since GPUs can do larger scatter/gather. But watch out: batching increases tail latency for individual users. Redwood's serving runtime supports continuous batching and can enforce per-request latency SLOs with early flush heuristics.

[00:08:05] Sasha: We also recommend prefix-aware batching: group requests that share the same prefix so route-cache hits and kv cache reuse happen more frequently. That's especially effective for chatapps with common system prompts.

[00:08:30] Ruth: On quantization — we want to move to 4-bit for cost reasons, but worried about hallucinations/regressions. Any guidance per model family?

[00:08:46] Priya: 8-bit usually safe with minimal regressions if you're using quant-aware kernels; 4-bit works but you need to test per-prompt evaluation harness. Mistral family models tend to be more robust to aggressive quant because of layernorm/order; Qwen sometimes needs per-layer remapping. We'll provide recommended quant profiles — layer groups that should remain FP16.

[00:09:18] Markus: Can you share those profiles? Also what about KV cache when using 4-bit — does cache still live FP16?

[00:09:32] Diego: In many setups the KV cache is stored in FP16 to keep attention kernel's compute path efficient. We sometimes store weights quantized but expand to FP16 at runtime for cache ops. That costs memory but retains numerical stability. There's a trade: store kv in 8-bit for memory but expect higher scattering/expansion cost.

[00:09:58] Anika: Let's dig into RoPE scaling specifically. At 4k tokens we saw Llama degrade around 3.5k unless they've patched RoPE. What options are there?

[00:10:12] Priya: Two main options: 1) use a RoPE-scaling patch — scale the rotary base to extend the interpolation for longer sequences; 2) use attention windowing / local attention for parts of the history. Scaling sometimes reduces precision on short contexts so it's a trade. For Llama you can see non-linear degradation unless you adjust the base. Mistral's smaller base frequencies can handle 4k better out-of-the-box. Qwen's implementation has specific numeric constants that can be tuned. We'll include plots.

[00:10:50] Ruth: If we patch RoPE, does that break instruction tuning or safety classifiers?

[00:11:02] Priya: Mostly not, but any param surgery should be validated. That's why we tie quality monitoring to prompt sets. Redwood Optimize can run regular evals against your golden prompts and trigger rollbacks if score drops.

[00:11:24] Sasha: Let's also talk about on-prem NIC contention. Markus, you mentioned your racks are 100GbE between nodes?

[00:11:36] Markus: Yeah, 100GbE, Mellanox, and some NVLink between GPUs on the same host but not across hosts.

[00:11:46] Diego: For MoE, if you do cross-host dispatch, the NIC becomes a bottleneck unless you reduce expert replicas. Our recommendation: colocate hottest experts on local GPUs to avoid cross-host traffic for the common prefixes. For cross-host traffic we use pinned NCCL rings and compression of messages (uint8) to reduce bandwidth. But that adds CPU/latency overhead.

[00:12:18] Anika: Any quick heuristics for when to use dedicated vs hosted? We're evaluating Redwood Dedicated too.

[00:12:28] Sasha: If your usage is predictable and you need control over HBM/replica placement, Dedicated or Private is good. Hosted works for fast ramp, but for MoE and 4k tokens on 40GB cards you often prefer Dedicated so you can tune placement and avoid noisy neighbors. Private is the move if you need VPC-only and strict KMS keys.

[00:12:52] Ruth: Security: we will need SOC2 + KMS and audit logs for any trial. Do you support bringing your own HSM?

[00:13:03] Sasha: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations and audit logging. We'll send the security pack.

[00:13:18] Diego: Back to routing: another trick is top-k gating with load-balancing losses during training so experts are more uniformly used. At inference time you can set a capacity factor to cap how many tokens per expert; that avoids hot-expert tails but increases drop/overflow and therefore you may need fallback experts or a dense bypass.

[00:13:50] Markus: What's the runtime fallback behavior? If an expert overflows, do you reroute to another expert synchronously?

[00:14:01] Priya: Common approach is synchronous overflow to a fallback expert or to use a small dense FFN path. Redwood's runtime supports either: you can configure overflow to reroute to a backup expert or to do a dense fallback with slightly lower quality but bounded latency. We can demo these behaviors in the trial.

[00:14:26] Anika: I want an example: if we have MoE with 64 experts and top-2 gating, how much memory and bandwidth are we talking per token?

[00:14:38] Diego: Rough estimate: gating MLP is small, say 2x hidden dims * sizeof(float) per token for compute. Dispatch dominates: top-2 means 2 copies of each token's k/v go to two experts; so memory traffic scales roughly with num_experts_chosen * seq_len * hidden * sizeof(dtype). Hard to give exact without model dims but expect 1.6x-2.2x the memory movement vs dense model for the same seq. We'll put numbers in the spreadsheet.

[00:15:12] Ruth: Let's pivot to batching — you mentioned continuous batching. How aggressive can we be without breaking p95 targets?

[00:15:25] Diego: Continuous batching with SLOs allows you to set max buffer delay, e.g., 20-50ms. If your p95 SLO is 150ms, you can buffer 20-30ms to get 2-4x throughput improvements. For MoE, the batching helps more because dispatch kernels are amortized. There's no one-size-fits-all — need to tune per-workload.

[00:15:55] Anika: What about RPC vs REST — any perf diff we should know?

[00:16:05] Diego: gRPC with streaming tends to be lower overhead for high QPS but both are supported. Streaming is a big win for long-running token streams because you can flush partial tokens.

[00:16:22] Sasha: Quick note on kernels — some kernels are optimized for rotary attention with fused ops and are far faster than naive matmuls; choose the runtime kernel based on model pattern (e.g., multihead dims, kv layout). Redwood's runtime picks kernels automatically but you can override.

[00:16:42] Priya: Also watch for sequence length switching: if you mostly serve 512 but have rare 4k floods, kernel caches and memory pools can thrash. We recommend warmup runs for long seq lengths to pre-allocate KV pools.

[00:17:05] Markus: Any known Qwen-specific gotchas? We saw some numeric stability at high seqs and weird tokens.

[00:17:15] Priya: Qwen sometimes uses a slightly different rotary scaling constant and layernorm ordering; when people port Qwen into generic runtimes they lose some numeric fidelity unless they match the original ops. We'll provide a checklist of matching layernorm epsilon, rotary base, and no-op reorderings.

[00:17:40] Anika: This is great, can we see the perf spreadsheet you mentioned?

[00:17:46] Sasha: We'll share the spreadsheet after the call. It will include measured p50/p95/p99, bytes moved, gating overhead, and memory footprints per seq for Llama-13B, Mistral-7B, Qwen-7B, and a MoE-variant.

[00:18:10] Markus: Will you include example Redwood config snippets for route-cache and expert-replica hints?

[00:18:18] Diego: Yes. Example: route_cache: {enabled: true, ttl_ms: 300000, key: prefix_hash} and expert_replica_hint: {hot_experts: [2,5,11], replicate_locally: true}. Those are high-level; the yaml will be in the doc.

[00:18:37] Ruth: About evaluations — how do we validate no regression after quant or RoPE patching?

[00:18:45] Priya: Redwood Optimize supports prompt-based evals + rollout gates. You specify golden prompt sets and metrics (e.g., accuracy, toxicity, F1 on specific tasks). If a deployment causes regression beyond threshold, rollback automatically to previous model variant.

[00:19:05] Anika: Any risk with using route-cache from a security/data standpoint? Does it persist content?

[00:19:14] Sasha: Route-cache only stores routing logits/selectors (small, non-user content). KV cache contains user tokens and is subject to data-retention policies. On Private, you control retention and KMS. We'll send security docs that separate route metadata from token storage.

[00:19:38] Markus: Ok next — actionable perf tests. Diego, what exactly will you run from our sample payloads?

[00:19:46] Diego: We'll run four runs per model: dense baseline, MoE with route-cache enabled, MoE with route-cache disabled, and MoE with dense-fallback overflow. Each run at seq lens 512/2048/4096, batch sizes [1,4,8]. We'll collect p50/p95/p99, GPU-util, bytes_sent, and expert-utilization.

[00:20:10] Anika: Sounds perfect. Can you give an expected timeline for results?

[00:20:16] Diego: We'll do a first pass in 5 business days and share raw spreadsheet; full plots in 9 business days. We noted that in action items.

[00:20:30] Ruth: Anything else about deployment? We might want a small private footprint, like 4 GPUs, to prototype. Will Redwood Private support that?

[00:20:40] Sasha: Yes, we support small clusters. For MoE it's tight on 4 GPUs unless you use smaller model families or reduce seq lengths. We'll map options in the trial proposal.

[00:21:02] Anika: A few tangents: compression of kv during transfer, checkpoint sharding for hot restarts, any quick notes?

[00:21:12] Diego: KV compression reduces bandwidth at the cost of CPU time; we use fast quant-compress (uint8) sometimes. For checkpoint sharding we prefer overlapping shards so a single host can warm up without full restore. It's all in the ops playbook we'll send.

[00:21:36] Sasha: Let's open the floor for quick clarifying questions.

[00:21:44] Ruth: Are there known copyright or licensing issues with Mistral/Qwen families on inference?

[00:21:52] Priya: Licensing varies; Redwood maintains a model-catalog that flags license compatibility. We'll include the catalog entries for each model we test.

[00:22:05] Anika: When we run your trial do we need to supply HSM credentials in advance?

[00:22:13] Sasha: For Private trials we can do an initial eval without HSM but for production you'll want to bring KMS. We'll make it optional for trial.

[00:22:26] Markus: Can you show an example of p99 vs expert-utilization graph? I want to understand tail correlation.

[00:22:36] Priya: We'll include that. Typically high expert skew correlates with worse p99 because overflow and async reroutes cause spikes. Uniformized experts -> lower tail but slightly higher average compute.

[00:22:58] Sasha: Great. We'll recap next steps at the end. Any final points?

[00:23:06] Anika: One last ask — can you include a short sanity-check config that keeps model dense but simulates MoE-like capacity via widened layers? We want to compare quality vs cost without full MoE complexity.

[00:23:20] Diego: We can do widened dense FFN comparisons; we'll add them to the spreadsheet.

[00:23:28] Sasha: Okay let's move to the wrap. Recap: Redwood will run benchmarks (Diego), Priya will prepare RoPE scaling plots and research notes, Sasha will send security & config docs and schedule a private trial. HelmEdge will provide payloads and infra details.

[00:23:50] Markus: We'll get infra topology and example traffic by Thursday.

[00:24:00] Sasha: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the perf spreadsheet and a meeting invite for the trial kickoff. End of notes.

(Transcript contains typical voice transcription artifacts: some names misrecognized, occasional filler words and overlaps.)
